title: Judges 6:25–32
context: Judges 6:25–32 records Gideon’s first act: at the LORD’s command he tears down his father’s altar of Baal, cuts down the Asherah beside it, and builds an altar to the LORD on which he offers his father’s bull. Afraid of his family and town, he does it at night with ten servants. The townsmen demand his death, but Joash answers that if Baal is a god, he can contend for himself, and Gideon is named Jerub-Baal ("Let Baal contend"). Both traditions see reform beginning at home and the LORD exposing the powerlessness of the idol.

verses.text: That same night, the LORD said to him, “Take your father’s bull, even the second bull seven years old, and throw down the altar of Baal that your father has, and cut down the Asherah that is by it.
verses.arminianNotes: That night the LORD tells Gideon to take his father’s bull, throw down his father’s altar of Baal, and cut down the Asherah beside it. Arminians see the call to reform beginning at home, where Gideon must choose loyalty to the LORD over family idolatry.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and stress that before God delivers Israel from Midian he deals with the idolatry behind the oppression. Both traditions read the command as a call to exclusive worship of the LORD, the issue raised by the prophet in 6:10.

verses.text: Then build an altar to the LORD your God on the top of this stronghold, in an orderly way, and take the second bull, and offer a burnt offering with the wood of the Asherah which you shall cut down.”
verses.arminianNotes: Gideon is to build an altar to the LORD on the stronghold in proper order and burn the second bull with the wood of the Asherah. Arminians see a public turning from idols to the LORD, with the idol’s own wood used for true worship.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree and note that the details of the bull and the phrase "second bull" are uncertain. Both traditions see the reversal in burning the Asherah to worship the LORD as a statement of his supremacy.

verses.text: Then Gideon took ten men of his servants, and did as the LORD had spoken to him. Because he feared his father’s household and the men of the city, he could not do it by day, but he did it by night.
verses.arminianNotes: Gideon takes ten servants and does as the LORD said, but at night because he fears his family and the townsmen. Arminian readers see real obedience mixed with fear, and they note that God works through Gideon’s partial courage.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and observe that the text records his fear honestly without condemning it. Both traditions see God’s patience with weak faith and see the obedience itself as what matters, even though it is done in hiding.

verses.text: When the men of the city arose early in the morning, behold, the altar of Baal was broken down, and the Asherah was cut down that was by it, and the second bull was offered on the altar that was built.
verses.arminianNotes: The townsmen rise early and find Baal’s altar broken down, the Asherah cut down, and the bull offered on the new altar. Arminians see the act as a public challenge to the town’s idolatry, which forces the people to face the question of who is God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree and note that the verse repeats the details of 6:25–26 to show the command was carried out fully. Both traditions see the scene as confronting a town that had adopted Baal worship.

verses.text: They said to one another, “Who has done this thing?” When they inquired and asked, they said, “Gideon the son of Joash has done this thing.”
verses.arminianNotes: The townsmen ask who did it and learn that Gideon son of Joash did it. Arminian readers note that obedience done at night cannot stay hidden, and Gideon must now face the consequences publicly.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the inquiry as preparing for Joash’s response. Both traditions note the irony that the Israelite townsmen are more upset about Baal’s altar than about the LORD’s covenant, which shows how deep the idolatry had gone.

verses.text: Then the men of the city said to Joash, “Bring out your son, that he may die, because he has broken down the altar of Baal, and because he has cut down the Asherah that was by it.”
verses.arminianNotes: The men of the city demand that Joash bring out his son to be killed for destroying Baal’s altar and the Asherah. Arminians see how far Israel had fallen: the law’s penalty for idolatry (Deuteronomy 13:6–10) is turned against the man who removed an idol.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree and see the reversal as an indictment of the town. Both traditions read the demand as showing the danger Gideon faced and the depth of Israel’s apostasy before God’s deliverance.

verses.text: Joash said to all who stood against him, “Will you contend for Baal? Or will you save him? He who will contend for him, let him be put to death by morning! If he is a god, let him contend for himself, because someone has broken down his altar!”
verses.arminianNotes: Joash asks whether they will contend for Baal and says that if Baal is a god, let him contend for himself. Arminian readers see Joash, whose altar it was, changing sides and exposing the foolishness of defending a god who cannot defend himself.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the argument anticipating Elijah’s challenge on Carmel (1 Kings 18:27). Both traditions read Joash’s words as a confession that an idol that needs human defense is no god, whatever his motives may have been.

verses.text: Therefore on that day he named him Jerub-Baal, saying, “Let Baal contend against him, because he has broken down his altar.”
verses.arminianNotes: Gideon is named Jerub-Baal, which the WEB footnote says means "Let Baal contend." Arminians see the name as a lasting reminder that Baal could not act against the man who tore down his altar.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree. Elsewhere the name appears as Jerubbesheth (2 Samuel 11:21), with "Baal" replaced. Both traditions read the name as a memorial of the LORD’s superiority over Baal.
